title: Ice floats because freezing locks water molecules further apart
body: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock its V-shaped molecules into an open, hexagonal lattice with more empty space than the jostling liquid. So a litre of water becomes about 1.09 litres of ice, and ice is about 8.3% less dense: 0.9167 g/cm³ against about 0.9998 g/cm³ for water at 0 °C. Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C, so in winter that water sinks to the bottom of a lake while colder water stays on top and freezes there. The floating ice then shelters the water beneath, where plants and animals live through the winter.

slides.question: Freeze exactly 1 litre of water. About how much ice do you get?
slides.explanation: About 1,090 mL. Water expands by about 9% as it freezes, because hydrogen bonds hold its molecules apart in an open lattice.

slides.alt: Animation: an ice cube floats in a glass, and a litre of water freezes into 1.09 litres of ice. V-shaped water molecules tumble, then lock into a hexagonal lattice with dashed hydrogen bonds. A balance weighs water against ice, and a lake cools to 4 °C at the bottom while ice forms on top.

slides.heading: Densest at 4 °C
slides.text: Most liquids get denser as they cool. Water does too, but only down to about 4 °C. Colder than that, the molecules start to line up as they will in ice, and the water gets lighter again.

slides.heading: Density of water and ice
slides.note: Ice is about 8.3% less dense than the water it floats on.

slides.heading: Burst pipes and cracked rocks
slides.text: Freezing water expands with great force. It bursts water pipes, and repeated freezing and thawing splits rocks and lifts and cracks roads, a process called frost heaving.

slides.heading: A tiny club
slides.text: Only a handful of other substances also expand when they freeze, among them silicon, gallium, germanium and bismuth.

slides.question: Why does the bottom of a deep, frozen lake stay at about 4 °C?
options: The ice traps heat from the Sun
Mud on the lake bed gives off heat
slides.explanation: Water near 4 °C is the densest, so it sinks and stays at the bottom. Colder, lighter water stays on top, where it freezes into a floating lid.
